claim: DYT25 (Gnal+/−) mice carry a heterozygous knockout mutation of the Gnal gene.
source: DYT25 (Gnal+/−) mice carry a heterozygous knockout mutation of the Gnal gene, which notably disrupts striatal function, and systemic or striatal administration of oxotremorine to these mice triggers dystonic symptoms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to Pelosi et al., 2017 throughout the manuscript describing the mouse model.

claim: The Gnal gene mutation notably disrupts striatal function in DYT25 mice.
source: DYT25 (Gnal+/−) mice carry a heterozygous knockout mutation of the Gnal gene, which notably disrupts striatal function, and systemic or striatal administration of oxotremorine to these mice triggers dystonic symptoms.
evidence: Referenced to prior work (Pelosi et al., 2017) establishing striatal dysfunction in this model.

claim: Systemic or striatal administration of oxotremorine to Gnal+/− mice triggers dystonic symptoms.
source: DYT25 (Gnal+/−) mice carry a heterozygous knockout mutation of the Gnal gene, which notably disrupts striatal function, and systemic or striatal administration of oxotremorine to these mice triggers dystonic symptoms.
evidence: This is a key finding from Pelosi et al., 2017 that is replicated in the current study.

claim: Gnal+/− mice exhibit increased cerebello-thalamic excitability in the presymptomatic state.
source: Our results reveal an increased cerebello-thalamic excitability in the presymptomatic state.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Following the first dystonic episode, Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state exhibit a further increase of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical excitability.
source: Following the first dystonic episode, Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state exhibit a further increase of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical excitability, which is maintained after θ-burst stimulations of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 'Post-Oxo' condition data in Figure 2C showing increased responses compared to naive condition.

claim: The increased cerebello-thalamo-cortical excitability in asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice is maintained after θ-burst stimulations of the cerebellum.
source: Following the first dystonic episode, Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state exhibit a further increase of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical excitability, which is maintained after θ-burst stimulations of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 where θ-burst stimulations fail to induce potentiation in Gnal+/- mice in saline condition.

claim: θ-burst stimulations of the cerebellum administered in the symptomatic state decreased the cerebello-thalamic excitability in Gnal+/- mice.
source: When administered in the symptomatic state induced by a cholinergic activation, these stimulations decreased the cerebello-thalamic excitability and reduced dystonic symptoms.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5E-F showing depression of responses after θ-burst in oxotremorine condition.

claim: θ-burst stimulations of the cerebellum administered in the symptomatic state reduced dystonic symptoms in Gnal+/- mice.
source: When administered in the symptomatic state induced by a cholinergic activation, these stimulations decreased the cerebello-thalamic excitability and reduced dystonic symptoms.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H-I with decreased dystonia scores and increased active wake after θ-burst stimulations.

claim: The increased cerebello-thalamic excitability constitutes an early endophenotype in DYT25 dystonia.
source: In agreement with dystonia being a multiregional circuit disorder, our results suggest that the increased cerebello-thalamic excitability constitutes an early endophenotype, and that the cerebellum is a gateway for corrective therapies via the depression of cerebello-thalamic pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding of increased excitability in presymptomatic mice (Figure 2) that is further amplified after the first episode.

claim: The cerebellum is a gateway for corrective therapies via the depression of cerebello-thalamic pathways in DYT25 dystonia.
source: In agreement with dystonia being a multiregional circuit disorder, our results suggest that the increased cerebello-thalamic excitability constitutes an early endophenotype, and that the cerebellum is a gateway for corrective therapies via the depression of cerebello-thalamic pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the therapeutic effect of θ-burst stimulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dystonia is characterized by involuntary movements and abnormal postures caused by the co-contraction of antagonistic muscles.
source: Dystonia is a class of neurological disease whose symptomatology is characterized by involuntary movements and abnormal postures, caused by the co-contraction of antagonistic muscles (Berardelli et al., 1998; Albanese et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: The wide clinical spectrum of dystonia has hampered the identification of a common pathophysiological mechanism underlying the disease.
source: The wide clinical spectrum of dystonia, whether in causes or clinical manifestations, has hampered so far the identification of a common pathophysiological mechanism underlying the disease (Balint et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citation.

claim: Early studies have primarily highlighted the role of the basal ganglia in the onset of dystonia.
source: If early studies have primarily highlighted the role of the basal ganglia in the onset of the disease, more recent studies have revealed strong dysfunctions in the motor cortex, thalamus, and cerebellum in dystonic patients, questioning which structural impairments are primary or secondary causes of dystonia (Simonyan, 2018).
evidence: This is a historical statement about the field supported by citation.

claim: Recent studies have revealed strong dysfunctions in the motor cortex, thalamus, and cerebellum in dystonic patients.
source: If early studies have primarily highlighted the role of the basal ganglia in the onset of the disease, more recent studies have revealed strong dysfunctions in the motor cortex, thalamus, and cerebellum in dystonic patients, questioning which structural impairments are primary or secondary causes of dystonia (Simonyan, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: Lesions in the basal ganglia or cerebellum do not systematically induce a dystonic phenotype.
source: Indeed, lesions in the basal ganglia or in the cerebellum do not systematically induce a dystonic phenotype, and the onset of the disease is usually delayed following the lesions.
evidence: This is an observation from the literature about the relationship between lesions and dystonia.

claim: The onset of dystonia is usually delayed following lesions in the basal ganglia or cerebellum.
source: Indeed, lesions in the basal ganglia or in the cerebellum do not systematically induce a dystonic phenotype, and the onset of the disease is usually delayed following the lesions.
evidence: This is an observation from clinical literature.

claim: Approaches targeting the basal ganglia and cerebellum have yielded inconsistent outcomes in dystonia treatment.
source: Moreover, if the basal ganglia and cerebellum have been considered as therapeutic targets, approaches targeting these structures yielded inconsistent outcomes (Oyama and Hattori, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of therapeutic approaches.

claim: Dystonia is a circuit disorder that has a diversity of triggering mechanisms but requires the interactions between several nodes of the motor network to reach a symptomatic state.
source: These specificities led to the emergence of a new working hypothesis, that dystonia is a circuit disorder that has a diversity of triggering mechanisms but requires the interactions between several nodes of the motor network to reach a symptomatic state (Lehéricy et al., 2013; Prudente et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: Nonmanifesting DYT1 mutation carriers exhibit altered temporal discrimination threshold.
source: In line with the circuit disorder theory, studies of genetic forms of the disease have identified endophenotypes in the form of nonmotor symptoms, such as altered temporal discrimination threshold in nonmanifesting mutation carriers (Hutchinson et al., 2013), causing an inability of individuals to consider two subsequent stimuli as asynchronous if those are presented in a short amount of time.
evidence: This is cited from the literature as an example of an endophenotype.

claim: Anomalies in synaptic plasticity in the cortex and striatum have been linked to dystonia in genetic forms of dystonia in rodent models.
source: Anomalies in synaptic plasticity in the cortex and striatum have also been linked to dystonia in genetic forms of dystonia in rodent models (Calabresi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a review of rodent model studies.

claim: Nonmanifesting DYT6 mice exhibit aberrant electrophysiological activity in the cerebellar cortex and nuclei.
source: Cerebellar dysfunction preexisting to symptoms has also been observed in such models: nonmanifesting DYT6 mice exhibit an aberrant electrophysiological activity in the cerebellar cortex and nuclei, which is further disrupted in manifesting animals (van der Heijden et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from a recent study on DYT6 mice.

claim: DYT1 mutation carriers exhibit cerebello-thalamic disruptions.
source: Indeed, DYT1 mutation carriers exhibit cerebello-thalamic disruptions, and the penetrance of DYT1 dystonia, as well as the severity of symptoms, is regulated by the structural integrity of cerebello-thalamo-cortical tracts (Argyelan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from a neuroimaging study in DYT1 patients.

claim: The penetrance of DYT1 dystonia and the severity of symptoms are regulated by the structural integrity of cerebello-thalamo-cortical tracts.
source: Indeed, DYT1 mutation carriers exhibit cerebello-thalamic disruptions, and the penetrance of DYT1 dystonia, as well as the severity of symptoms, is regulated by the structural integrity of cerebello-thalamo-cortical tracts (Argyelan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from a neuroimaging study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Cerebello-thalamic disruptions have been reproduced in a mouse model of DYT1.
source: This observation has been reproduced in a mouse model of DYT1 (Uluğ et al., 2011), as well as a defect in cortico-striatal plasticity (Yu-Taeger et al., 2020), supporting the possibility of an inter-dependence of cerebello-thalamic and striatal dysfunctions.
evidence: This is cited from studies in DYT1 mouse models.

claim: DYT1 mouse models exhibit a defect in cortico-striatal plasticity.
source: This observation has been reproduced in a mouse model of DYT1 (Uluğ et al., 2011), as well as a defect in cortico-striatal plasticity (Yu-Taeger et al., 2020), supporting the possibility of an inter-dependence of cerebello-thalamic and striatal dysfunctions.
evidence: This is cited from a study on DYT1 mice.

claim: DYT25 is a recently identified genetic form of primary torsion dystonia characterized as an autosomal-dominant adult-onset disorder.
source: DYT25 is a recently identified genetic form of primary torsion dystonia, characterized as an autosomal-dominant adult-onset disorder (Fuchs et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from the initial reports identifying DYT25.

claim: DYT25 is caused by loss-of-function mutations of the Gnal gene encoding Gα(olf).
source: It is caused by loss-of-function mutations of the Gnal gene encoding Gα(olf), a G-protein stimulating adenylate cyclase activity, mainly expressed in the olfactory bulb and striatum, with a sparse expression in Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex (Belluscio et al., 1998; Vemula et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from studies characterizing the genetic basis of DYT25.

claim: Gα(olf) is a G-protein stimulating adenylate cyclase activity.
source: It is caused by loss-of-function mutations of the Gnal gene encoding Gα(olf), a G-protein stimulating adenylate cyclase activity, mainly expressed in the olfactory bulb and striatum, with a sparse expression in Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex (Belluscio et al., 1998; Vemula et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of Gα(olf) cited from the literature.

claim: Gα(olf) is mainly expressed in the olfactory bulb and striatum, with sparse expression in Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex.
source: It is caused by loss-of-function mutations of the Gnal gene encoding Gα(olf), a G-protein stimulating adenylate cyclase activity, mainly expressed in the olfactory bulb and striatum, with a sparse expression in Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex (Belluscio et al., 1998; Vemula et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from expression studies of Gα(olf).

claim: In the Gnal+/− mouse model, cAMP production is reduced in the striatum.
source: In this model, cAMP production is reduced in the striatum, disrupting striatal functions, but the mice are devoid of dystonic symptoms in early adulthood.
evidence: This is a finding from the characterization of the Gnal+/− mouse model (Pelosi et al., 2017).

claim: Gnal+/− mice are devoid of dystonic symptoms in early adulthood.
source: In this model, cAMP production is reduced in the striatum, disrupting striatal functions, but the mice are devoid of dystonic symptoms in early adulthood.
evidence: This is a key characteristic of the model cited from Pelosi et al., 2017.

claim: Dystonic symptoms in Gnal+/− mice are induced by injections of oxotremorine M administered either systemically or in the striatum, but not in the cerebellum.
source: In agreement with a role of increased striatal cholinergic activity in dystonia (Pisani et al., 2007), dystonic symptoms are induced by injections of a muscarinic cholinergic agonist (oxotremorine M) administered either systemically or in the striatum, but not in the cerebellum, and were prevented by the muscarinic antagonist, trihexyphenidyl, a drug alleviating symptoms in many dystonic patients.
evidence: This is a finding from Pelosi et al., 2017 characterizing the inducibility of dystonia in the model.

claim: Dystonic symptoms in Gnal+/− mice were prevented by the muscarinic antagonist trihexyphenidyl.
source: In agreement with a role of increased striatal cholinergic activity in dystonia (Pisani et al., 2007), dystonic symptoms are induced by injections of a muscarinic cholinergic agonist (oxotremorine M) administered either systemically or in the striatum, but not in the cerebellum, and were prevented by the muscarinic antagonist, trihexyphenidyl, a drug alleviating symptoms in many dystonic patients.
evidence: This is cited from Pelosi et al., 2017.

claim: An increase in striatal cholinergic tone is critical to the onset of dystonia in Gnal+/− mice.
source: This indicates that an increase in striatal cholinergic tone is critical to the onset of the disorder (Pelosi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation from Pelosi et al., 2017 based on the pharmacological induction experiments.

claim: Similar alterations in cortico-striatal plasticity were observed in DYT1 and DYT25 animal models.
source: Strikingly, in animal models, similar alterations in cortico-striatal plasticity were observed in DYT1 and DYT25, suggesting common pathophysiological mechanisms (Martella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from a comparative study of DYT1 and DYT25 models.

claim: The alteration of cerebellum or cerebello-thalamic tracts has been linked to the expression of DYT1 in patients and mouse models.
source: While the alteration of cerebellum or cerebello-thalamic tracts has been linked to the expression of DYT1 in patients and mouse models (Argyelan et al., 2009; Uluğ et al., 2011; Fremont et al., 2017), studies of DYT25 have remained focused on striatal alterations.
evidence: This is cited from multiple studies on DYT1.

claim: Studies of DYT25 have remained focused on striatal alterations.
source: While the alteration of cerebellum or cerebello-thalamic tracts has been linked to the expression of DYT1 in patients and mouse models (Argyelan et al., 2009; Uluğ et al., 2011; Fremont et al., 2017), studies of DYT25 have remained focused on striatal alterations.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the literature on DYT25.

claim: Cerebellar stimulations have been shown to be beneficial in idiopathic cervical dystonia.
source: Moreover, cerebellar stimulations have been shown to be beneficial in idiopathic cervical dystonia (Koch et al., 2014; Bradnam et al., 2016), and genetic mouse models of dystonia allow a finer dissection of the effects induced by this type of approach (van der Heijden et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from clinical studies of cerebellar stimulation.

claim: Young adult Gnal+/- mice (3-7 months old) do not exhibit constitutive locomotor impairments.
source: 3–7-month-old Gnal+/- mice have been described as asymptomatic, without dystonic phenotype in control conditions (Pelosi et al., 2017). To further examine whether Gnal+/- mice exhibit constitutive motor deficit (taking into account gender), we performed a larger set of motor experiments, including vertical pole, horizontal bar, grid test, fixed-speed rotarod, gait test, and an open-field test (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral tests shown in Figure 1 showing no significant differences between genotypes.

claim: The motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test.
source: We observed that the motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1a), horizontal bar test (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1a), and grid test (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with no significant differences between genotypes.

claim: The motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the horizontal bar test.
source: We observed that the motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1a), horizontal bar test (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1a), and grid test (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with no significant differences between genotypes.

claim: The motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the grid test.
source: We observed that the motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1a), horizontal bar test (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1a), and grid test (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with no significant differences between genotypes.

claim: Females exhibited better performances in the horizontal bar test, regardless of their genotype.
source: Females exhibited better performances in the horizontal bar test, regardless of their genotype.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1B showing a gender effect independent of genotype.

claim: No significant differences were found between Gnal+/- and WT mice in the fixed-speed rotarod test.
source: Motor coordination was also examined in a fixed-speed rotarod test. We did not find significant differences between Gnal+/- and WT mice (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1a), nor when comparing males and females for each speed step (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D-E with no significant differences.

claim: No significant differences were found in gait width, alternation coefficient, linear movement, sigma, or length of stride in the gait test between Gnal+/- and WT mice.
source: In the gait test, we found no significant differences in gait width, alternation coefficient, linear movement, sigma, or length of stride (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with no significant differences across multiple gait parameters.

claim: No significant differences were observed between genotype and gender in median instantaneous speed or distance traveled in the open field.
source: Finally, in spontaneous locomotion in the open field, we observed no significant differences between genotype and gender neither in median instantaneous speed nor in distance traveled (Figure 1G, J and K, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1J-K with no significant differences.

claim: No significant differences were observed between genotypes or genders in thigmotaxis and time spent exploring the center of the open field.
source: Additionally, we included an analysis of the thigmotaxis and time spent exploring the center of the open field and observed no significant differences between genotypes or genders in our mice (Figure 1H, I, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H-I with no significant differences.

claim: Motor activity and motor coordination are not impaired in young 3–7-month-old Gnal+/- mice.
source: In conclusion, motor activity and motor coordination are not impaired in young 3–7-month-old Gnal+/- mice; furthermore, no significant differences were observed between male and female Gnal+/- mice compared to their WT littermates, allowing us to merge genders in the following physiological experiments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the behavioral tests shown in Figure 1.

claim: No significant differences were observed between male and female Gnal+/- mice compared to their WT littermates in motor tests.
source: In conclusion, motor activity and motor coordination are not impaired in young 3–7-month-old Gnal+/- mice; furthermore, no significant differences were observed between male and female Gnal+/- mice compared to their WT littermates, allowing us to merge genders in the following physiological experiments.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of gender effects across all behavioral tests in Figure 1.

claim: VAL, CL, and M1 neurons presented no differences in firing rate between WT and Gnal+/- mice in basal conditions.
source: VAL, CL, and M1 neurons presented no differences in firing rate between WT and Gnal+/- mice in basal conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A comparing baseline firing rates.

claim: Oxotremorine treatment induces in both WT and Gnal+/- mice a cholinergic shock, which translates into excessive salivation and lacrimation, as well as a persistent immobility.
source: As described previously, this treatment induces in both genotypes a cholinergic shock, which translates into excessive salivation and lacrimation, as well as a persistent immobility.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral effects of oxotremorine administration.

claim: Oxotremorine induces in Gnal+/- mice abnormal dystonic-like movements and postures.
source: It also induces in Gnal+/- mice abnormal dystonic-like movements and postures.
evidence: This is observed in the behavioral assessment and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Oxotremorine-treated mice presented a significant decrease in the firing rate of VAL and M1 neurons.
source: Oxotremorine-treated mice, whether WT or Gnal+/-, presented a significant decrease in the firing rate of VAL and M1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A comparing firing rates before and after oxotremorine.

claim: Oxotremorine did not modify the firing properties of CL neurons in WT mice.
source: While oxotremorine did not modify the firing properties of CL neurons in WT mice, it decreased the firing rate of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A with a genotype-specific effect in CL.

claim: Oxotremorine decreased the firing rate of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice.
source: While oxotremorine did not modify the firing properties of CL neurons in WT mice, it decreased the firing rate of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Oxotremorine decreased the CVisi of VAL neurons in both WT and Gnal+/- mice.
source: We observed a significant decrease in CVisi of VAL neurons in both WT and Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1o and p).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A measuring firing regularity.

claim: Oxotremorine did not modify the CVisi of CL neurons in WT mice.
source: While oxotremorine did not modify the CVisi of CL neurons in WT mice, it was decreased for CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1o and p), suggesting an increased regularity of firing.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Oxotremorine decreased the CVisi of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice, suggesting an increased regularity of firing.
source: While oxotremorine did not modify the CVisi of CL neurons in WT mice, it was decreased for CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1o and p), suggesting an increased regularity of firing.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A with interpretation of the CVisi decrease.

claim: The DN is the main output of the cerebellum towards the thalamus.
source: The DN is the main output of the cerebellum towards the thalamus and is known to project both to the VAL and CL (Ichinohe et al., 2000; Teune et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: The DN projects to both the VAL and CL.
source: The DN is the main output of the cerebellum towards the thalamus and is known to project both to the VAL and CL (Ichinohe et al., 2000; Teune et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: In naive saline-treated mice, VAL, CL thalamus and M1 neurons displayed significant departure from baseline firing during 100 ms DN stimulations in both WT and Gnal+/- mice.
source: In naive saline-treated mice, we found a significant increase in firing rate for the VAL, CL thalamus and M1 neurons during 100 ms DN stimulations in WT and Gnal+/-mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C demonstrating responses to DN stimulation.

claim: Responses in the VAL to DN stimulation were significantly larger in Gnal+/- than in WT mice in the presymptomatic state.
source: Responses in the VAL were significantly larger in Gnal+/- than in WT mice, suggesting an increased responsiveness of this thalamo-cortical pathway in the presymptomatic state.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C comparing genotypes.

claim: Low-frequency stimulation of the DN did not induce plastic changes of the responses in VAL, CL, and M1.
source: We verified the absence of plastic changes of the responses in VAL, CL, and M1 induced by our low-frequency stimulation of the DN by showing the absence of significant difference between the average response to the first half of the stimulations ('early') and the second half of the stimulations ('late,' Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and D, Supplementary file 1n).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D comparing early and late responses.

claim: The first exposure to oxotremorine does not cause significant short-term changes in the cerebellar drive of thalamic nuclei and motor cortex.
source: We did not observe any significant difference in response to DN stimulation in the VAL, CL, and M1 in comparison to naive condition, for both genotypes (Supplementary file 1c and d). This suggests that the first exposure to oxotremorine does not cause significant short-term changes in the cerebellar drive of thalamic nuclei and motor cortex.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of responses in the 'Oxo' condition to the naive condition.

claim: Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state (Post-Oxo) presented a significantly larger response to DN stimulations in all recorded structures compared to the changes induced by oxotremorine in WT animals.
source: While the acute exposure to oxotremorine yielded slightly increased responses in VAL neurons and decreased responses in M1 neurons in WT mice, Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state presented a significantly larger response to DN stimulations in all recorded structures compared to the changes induced by oxotremorine in WT animals (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1c and d), indicating an increased excitability of the cerebello-thalamic pathways in asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice following the first dystonia induction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C comparing Post-Oxo responses between genotypes.

claim: A single exposure of Gnal+/- mice to oxotremorine induces long-lasting functional alterations in the cerebello-thalamic pathways that are more pronounced than the mild alterations observed in the presymptomatic state.
source: Overall, these results show that a single exposure of Gnal+/- mice to oxotremorine induces, in the cerebello-thalamic pathways, long-lasting functional alterations that are more pronounced than the mild alterations observed in the presymptomatic state.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparison of naive and Post-Oxo conditions in Figure 2C.

claim: In saline-treated WT mice, θ-burst stimulations of the DN induced a potentiation of the response in VAL and M1 neurons to low-frequency stimulation.
source: In saline-treated WT mice, the comparison of the increase in firing rate induced by DN stimulations before and after θ-burst stimulations (Figure 3B and C) revealed a potentiation of the response in VAL and M1 neurons to the low-frequency stimulation (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D demonstrating potentiation in WT mice.

claim: In Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations failed to induce a significant potentiation in the responses of VAL, CL, or M1 neurons to DN stimulations in saline condition.
source: On the other hand, in Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations failed to induce a significant potentiation in the responses of VAL, CL, or M1 neurons to DN stimulations, yielding significantly smaller θ-burst-induced changes in response to DN stimulations compared to WT mice (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D comparing the effect of θ-burst between genotypes.

claim: θ-burst stimulations of the DN induced a potentiated response for WT mice in motor thalamo-cortical pathways in saline condition, whereas this potentiation was absent in Gnal+/- mice.
source: Hence, in the saline condition, θ-burst stimulations of the DN induced a potentiated response for WT mice in motor thalamo-cortical pathways, whereas this potentiation was absent in Gnal+/- mice, indicating an impaired plasticity of cerebello-thalamic pathways in the asymptomatic state.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The cerebello-CL-striatal pathway plays a central role in certain forms of dystonia.
source: The cerebello-CL-striatal pathway (Ichinohe et al., 2000; Bostan and Strick, 2010; Chen et al., 2014; Gornati et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018) has been shown to play a central role in certain forms of dystonia (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from studies on the cerebello-striatal pathway in dystonia.

claim: DN neurons exhibited a bimodal distribution of firing rate in the DLS, allowing separation of slow- and fast-spiking neurons corresponding to putative medium spiny neurons and interneurons.
source: DLS neurons exhibited a bimodal distribution of firing rate (Figure 4E), allowing to separate slow- and fast-spiking neurons corresponding to putative medium spiny neurons and interneurons (Her et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and based on established classification criteria cited from the literature.

claim: Neurons from both slow- and fast-spiking populations in the DLS displayed significant departure from baseline firing during DN optogenetic stimulations in both WT and Gnal+/- mice.
source: Neurons from both populations in the DLS displayed significant departure from baseline firing during DN optogenetic stimulations in both WT and Gnal+/- mice, but there was no significant increase in the firing rate of the population over the whole stimulation interval (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F demonstrating responses to DN-CL stimulation.

claim: θ-burst stimulations of the DN produced a rhythmic entrainment of the DLS fast-spiking populations.
source: Θ-burst stimulations of the DN also produced a rhythmic entrainment of the DLS fast-spiking populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C) consistent with a striatal entrainment through CL-projecting DN neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: In WT animals, DLS fast-spiking neurons exhibited increased responses to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations after θ-burst protocol.
source: In WT animals, DLS fast-spiking neurons exhibited increased responses to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations after θ-burst protocol, not only when taking into account the whole duration of the DN stimulation (Figure 4H and I), but also when focusing on the initial response (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I-J demonstrating potentiation in WT mice.

claim: θ-burst DN stimulations increase the recruitment of DLS fast-spiking units through an oligo-synaptic pathway in WT mice.
source: This suggests that θ-burst DN stimulations increase the recruitment of DLS fast-spiking units through an oligo-synaptic pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the potentiation observed in Figure 4I-J.

claim: The change in response to DN low-frequency 100 ms stimulations following θ-burst stimulations was absent in Gnal+/- mice in either type of units in the DLS.
source: In contrast, such change in response to DN low-frequency 100 ms stimulations was absent in Gnal+/- mice in either type of units in the DLS following θ-burst stimulations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I-J comparing the effect of θ-burst between genotypes.

claim: The observed difference between genotypes in striatal plasticity is consistent with the impact of θ-burst stimulations in the CL neurons in saline condition.
source: This observed difference between genotypes is consistent with the impact of θ-burst stimulations in the CL neurons in saline condition (Figure 3D and E) and thus indicates an impairment in cerebello-thalamo-striatal plasticity in asymptomatic ('post-Oxo') Gnal+/- mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the striatal findings to the thalamic findings.

claim: Following oxotremorine administration, the increase in firing rate in response to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1 neurons was stronger in Gnal+/- mice than WT mice.
source: Following oxotremorine administration, the increase in firing rate in response to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1 neurons was stronger in Gnal+/- mice than WT mice (Figure 5B), as also found in the asymptomatic condition (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B comparing responses between genotypes in oxotremorine condition.

claim: In WT mice, θ-burst stimulations under oxotremorine did not induce lasting changes in the response of VAL and M1 neurons to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations.
source: In WT mice, θ-burst stimulations under oxotremorine did not induce lasting changes in the response of VAL and M1 neurons to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations, neither when taking into account the whole duration of stimulation (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 1i), nor when looking only at the initial response ('afferent volley,' Figure 5F, Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E-F for WT mice in oxotremorine condition.

claim: θ-burst stimulations in Gnal+/- mice under oxotremorine induced a lasting depression of the response to low-frequency cerebellar stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1.
source: In contrast, θ-burst stimulations in Gnal+/- mice induced a lasting depression of the response to low-frequency cerebellar stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1 for the whole duration of the stimulation (Figure 5C–E, Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-E demonstrating depression in Gnal+/- mice.

claim: The depression of responses to DN stimulation after θ-burst in Gnal+/- mice under oxotremorine was also observed in the afferent volley.
source: This depression was also observed in the afferent volley (Figure 5F, Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F analyzing the initial response window.

claim: θ-bursts applied in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice induce a decrease in the entrainment of the thalamus and M1 by the cerebellum.
source: Thus, while cerebellar drive of the thalamus and cortex is enhanced in asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice, θ-bursts applied in symptomatic (but not asymptomatic, Figure 3E and F) Gnal+/- mice induce a decrease in the entrainment of the thalamus and M1 by the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings in Figure 5E-F compared to Figure 3.

claim: In Gnal+/- mice, oxotremorine consistently induced abnormal postures such as the extension of hind limbs from the body axis for >10 s, sustained hunched posture with little movements, slow walking with increased hind limb gait, yielding maximal dystonia scores.
source: In Gnal+/- mice, oxotremorine consistently induced abnormal postures such as the extension of hind limbs from the body axis for >10 s, sustained hunched posture with little movements, slow walking with increased hind limb gait, yielding maximal dystonia scores, while only mild motor signs were observed in WT mice (Figure 5H, Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G-H demonstrating the dystonic phenotype.

claim: Only mild motor signs were observed in WT mice following oxotremorine administration.
source: In Gnal+/- mice, oxotremorine consistently induced abnormal postures such as the extension of hind limbs from the body axis for >10 s, sustained hunched posture with little movements, slow walking with increased hind limb gait, yielding maximal dystonia scores, while only mild motor signs were observed in WT mice (Figure 5H, Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H comparing dystonia scores between genotypes.

claim: The surgical interventions (electrode and optical fiber implantation, AAV infections) did not impact the development of dystonic-type motor abnormalities in Gnal+/- mice.
source: These observations are consistent with the previous findings in Gnal+/- mice (Pelosi et al., 2017) and indicate that the surgical interventions (electrode and optical fiber implantation, AAV infections) did not impact the development of dystonic-type motor abnormalities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of the phenotype with prior reports.

claim: DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decreased the abnormal motor state in Gnal+/- mice following oxotremorine injection.
source: DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decreased the abnormal motor state in Gnal+/- mice following oxotremorine injection (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H comparing dystonia scores before and after θ-burst.

claim: In saline-treated WT mice, DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations had no significant effect on the active wake time.
source: In the saline-treated WT mice, DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations had no significant effect on the active wake time.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I for WT mice in saline condition.

claim: In asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations did not significantly change the percentage of time spent in active wake.
source: Similarly, in the asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations did not significantly change the percentage of time spent in active wake (Figure 5I, Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I for Gnal+/- mice in saline condition.

claim: In the oxotremorine condition, the average active wake time decreased in both WT and Gnal+/- mice compared to saline, the effect being more pronounced in the mutant mice.
source: In contrast, in the oxotremorine condition, the average active wake time decreased in both WT and Gnal+/- mice compared to saline, the effect being more pronounced in the mutant mice (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I comparing active wake between conditions.

claim: One session of DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulation was sufficient to increase the time spent in active wake in Gnal+/- mice under oxotremorine.
source: One session of DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulation was sufficient to increase the time spent in active wake in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 5I, Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I comparing active wake before and after θ-burst in oxotremorine condition.

claim: DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decrease the dystonic phenotype in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice regarding both the abnormal motor scores and active wake deficit.
source: Overall, these results indicate that DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decrease the dystonic phenotype in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice regarding both the abnormal motor scores and active wake deficit.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Young adult Gnal+/- mice in the presymptomatic state exhibit altered cerebello-thalamic functional connectivity without overt motor impairment.
source: Our results show that young adult Gnal+/- mice in the presymptomatic state, that is, without overt motor impairment, already exhibit altered cerebello-thalamic functional connectivity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: After the first dystonic episode, mutant animals in the asymptomatic state exhibit further functional alterations of the cerebello-thalamic pathways with a marked increase in cerebello-thalamic excitability.
source: After the first dystonic episode triggered by a cholinergic agonist, mutant animals, once returned to an asymptomatic state, exhibit further functional alterations of the cerebello-thalamic pathways, with a marked increase in cerebello-thalamic excitability and loss of potentiation of these functional connections by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations, which are also reflected downstream in the motor cortex and striatum.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: After the first dystonic episode, mutant animals in the asymptomatic state exhibit loss of potentiation of cerebello-thalamic functional connections by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations.
source: After the first dystonic episode triggered by a cholinergic agonist, mutant animals, once returned to an asymptomatic state, exhibit further functional alterations of the cerebello-thalamic pathways, with a marked increase in cerebello-thalamic excitability and loss of potentiation of these functional connections by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations, which are also reflected downstream in the motor cortex and striatum.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 demonstrating impaired plasticity.

claim: Cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state induce a functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway absent from control mice.
source: Finally, cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state induce a functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway absent from control mice, and this effect is accompanied by a reduction of the motor symptoms.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 demonstrating depression and symptom reduction.

claim: The functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway induced by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state is accompanied by a reduction of motor symptoms.
source: Finally, cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state induce a functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway absent from control mice, and this effect is accompanied by a reduction of the motor symptoms.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with both physiological and behavioral improvements.

claim: In Gnal+/- mice before the first dystonia episode, the cerebello-thalamic tract exhibits an increased excitability that is amplified after the first episode and can be seen as a functional endophenotype.
source: This shows that in Gnal+/- mice before the first dystonia episode the cerebello-thalamic tract exhibits an increased excitability that is amplified after the first episode and can thus be seen as a functional endophenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the progressive changes observed across conditions in Figure 2.

claim: The plasticity induced in the cerebello-thalamic pathway via cerebellar stimulations reducing the cerebello-thalamic excitability exerts an effective therapeutic potential.
source: Indeed, the plasticity induced in this pathway via cerebellar stimulations reducing the cerebello-thalamic excitability exerts an effective therapeutic potential.
evidence: This is based on the therapeutic effects shown in Figure 5.

claim: DYT25 is an adult-onset dystonia with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years).
source: DYT25 is known to be an adult-onset dystonia, with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years), and, although the onset occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%), dystonia can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases (Fuchs et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013; Dufke et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2014; Ziegan et al., 2014; Saunders-Pullman et al., 2014; Carecchio et al., 2016; Dos Santos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from multiple clinical reports on DYT25.

claim: The onset of DYT25 occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%).
source: DYT25 is known to be an adult-onset dystonia, with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years), and, although the onset occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%), dystonia can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases (Fuchs et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013; Dufke et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2014; Ziegan et al., 2014; Saunders-Pullman et al., 2014; Carecchio et al., 2016; Dos Santos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from clinical reports on DYT25.

claim: DYT25 can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases.
source: DYT25 is known to be an adult-onset dystonia, with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years), and, although the onset occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%), dystonia can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases (Fuchs et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013; Dufke et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2014; Ziegan et al., 2014; Saunders-Pullman et al., 2014; Carecchio et al., 2016; Dos Santos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from clinical reports on DYT25.

claim: Immunohistochemistry study in rats reveals Gα(olf) labeling in the olfactory bulb, striatum, substantia nigra, and cerebellar cortex.
source: Interestingly, the immunohistochemistry study in rats of Gα(olf), the protein encoded by Gnal, reveals labeling in the olfactory bulb, striatum, substantia nigra, and cerebellar cortex (Vemula et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from an expression study of Gα(olf).

claim: In the striatum, Gα(olf) is closely associated with the G protein subunits, Gγ7 and Gβ2, and the type 5 adenylyl cyclase (AC5) to form a multi-molecular complex critical for cAMP production.
source: In the striatum, Gα(olf) is closely associated with the G protein subunits, Gγ7 and Gβ2, and the type 5 adenylyl cyclase (AC5) to form a multi-molecular complex critical for cAMP production (Hervé, 2011; Xie et al., 2015) and mutations of Gγ7 and AC5 cause motor disorders, including dystonia, in animals and humans.
evidence: This is cited from studies on the molecular complex involving Gα(olf).

claim: Mutations of Gγ7 and AC5 cause motor disorders, including dystonia, in animals and humans.
source: In the striatum, Gα(olf) is closely associated with the G protein subunits, Gγ7 and Gβ2, and the type 5 adenylyl cyclase (AC5) to form a multi-molecular complex critical for cAMP production (Hervé, 2011; Xie et al., 2015) and mutations of Gγ7 and AC5 cause motor disorders, including dystonia, in animals and humans.
evidence: This is cited from studies on related genes in the same pathway.

claim: Homozygous Gγ7 knockout mice display age-dependent dystonia.
source: Homozygous Gγ7 knockout mice, which have a severe impairment of Gα(olf) signaling in the striatum, display age-dependent dystonia (Sasaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from a study on Gγ7 knockout mice.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of ADCY5 are responsible for chorea with dystonia.
source: In addition, loss-of-function mutations of ADCY5, the human gene encoding AC5, are responsible for chorea with dystonia (Carapito et al., 2015), whereas gain-of-function mutations cause dyskinesia with facial myokymia (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from genetic studies in humans.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations of ADCY5 cause dyskinesia with facial myokymia.
source: In addition, loss-of-function mutations of ADCY5, the human gene encoding AC5, are responsible for chorea with dystonia (Carapito et al., 2015), whereas gain-of-function mutations cause dyskinesia with facial myokymia (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from genetic studies in humans.

claim: The disruption of the striatal transduction pathway involving Gα(olf) likely plays a central role in the development of dystonia.
source: Thus, the disruption of the striatal transduction pathway involving Gα(olf) likely plays a central role in the development of dystonia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic evidence from multiple related genes.

claim: In the mouse striatum, expression of Gα(olf) highly increases between postnatal day 7 (P7) and P14.
source: In the mouse striatum, expression of Gα(olf) highly increases between postnatal day 7 (P7) and P14 (Iwamoto et al., 2004), a period during which motor skills of pups are developing intensely.
evidence: This is cited from a developmental expression study.

claim: The period between P7 and P14 is when motor skills of mouse pups are developing intensely.
source: In the mouse striatum, expression of Gα(olf) highly increases between postnatal day 7 (P7) and P14 (Iwamoto et al., 2004), a period during which motor skills of pups are developing intensely.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mouse motor development.

claim: Juvenile rats (P14) displayed intense staining of Gα(olf) in cell bodies of striatal cholinergic neurons and medium spiny neurons, while adult rats displayed a more diffused staining in the striatum with weaker staining in cholinergic neurons.
source: Moreover, while juvenile rats (P14) displayed intense staining in cell bodies of striatal cholinergic neurons and medium spiny neurons, adult rats displayed a more diffused staining in the striatum, with a weaker staining in cholinergic neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry studies cited earlier.

claim: Juvenile rats displayed staining of Gα(olf) in the soma and dendrites of Purkinje cells, while it was restricted to their soma in adult rats.
source: Similarly, juvenile rats displayed a staining of the soma and dendrites of Purkinje cells, while it was restricted to their soma in adult rats.
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry studies.

claim: Shifts in Gα(olf) expression suggest that it plays a role in shaping neuronal networks.
source: These shifts in expression suggest that Gα(olf) plays a role in shaping neuronal networks and that the mutation of Gnal may cause an abnormal neuronal circuit development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental expression patterns.

claim: The mutation of Gnal may cause an abnormal neuronal circuit development.
source: These shifts in expression suggest that Gα(olf) plays a role in shaping neuronal networks and that the mutation of Gnal may cause an abnormal neuronal circuit development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the developmental expression patterns.

claim: DYT25 is inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner, but the penetrance of the disease is only partial.
source: DYT25 is inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner, but the penetrance of the disease is only partial (Fuchs et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013), and the higher penetrance and earlier childhood onset in carriers of the homozygous mutation (Masuho et al., 2016) is consistent with a contribution of Gnal to the maturation of the motor system.
evidence: This is cited from genetic studies of DYT25.

claim: Carriers of the homozygous Gnal mutation exhibit higher penetrance and earlier childhood onset of dystonia.
source: DYT25 is inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner, but the penetrance of the disease is only partial (Fuchs et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013), and the higher penetrance and earlier childhood onset in carriers of the homozygous mutation (Masuho et al., 2016) is consistent with a contribution of Gnal to the maturation of the motor system.
evidence: This is cited from a genetic study.

claim: The higher penetrance and earlier onset in homozygous Gnal mutation carriers is consistent with a contribution of Gnal to the maturation of the motor system.
source: DYT25 is inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner, but the penetrance of the disease is only partial (Fuchs et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013), and the higher penetrance and earlier childhood onset in carriers of the homozygous mutation (Masuho et al., 2016) is consistent with a contribution of Gnal to the maturation of the motor system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genotype-phenotype correlation.

claim: Old (>1 year) Gnal+/- adult mice exhibit motor impairments and occasional dystonic-like posture.
source: While old (>1 year) Gnal+/- adult mice exhibit motor impairments and occasional dystonic-like posture (Pelosi et al., 2017), our results in young adult Gnal+/- mice failed to evidence motor deficits either in simple activities (locomotion and strength test) or in skilled movements (vertical rod, bar test, rotarod).
evidence: This is cited from Pelosi et al., 2017.

claim: Young adult Gnal+/- mice provide a model of the presymptomatic stage of dystonia.
source: They indeed provide a model of the presymptomatic stage of dystonia.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the absence of motor deficits in young mice shown in Figure 1.

claim: The tactile temporal discrimination threshold (TDT) is increased in different types of isolated dystonia, nonmanifesting DYT1-mutation carriers, and unaffected relatives of both familial and sporadic adult-onset dystonia patients.
source: The tactile temporal discrimination threshold (TDT) is increased in different types of isolated dystonia, nonmanifesting DYT1-mutation carriers, and unaffected relatives of both familial and sporadic adult-onset dystonia patients, and the somatotopic representation of fingers in the S1 cortex was disorganized on both sides in unilaterally affected dystonic patients (Meunier et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from studies on endophenotypes in dystonia.

claim: The somatotopic representation of fingers in the S1 cortex was disorganized on both sides in unilaterally affected dystonic patients.
source: The tactile temporal discrimination threshold (TDT) is increased in different types of isolated dystonia, nonmanifesting DYT1-mutation carriers, and unaffected relatives of both familial and sporadic adult-onset dystonia patients, and the somatotopic representation of fingers in the S1 cortex was disorganized on both sides in unilaterally affected dystonic patients (Meunier et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from a neuroimaging study.

claim: Inter-hemispheric inhibition is reduced in asymptomatic individuals with a family history of dystonia.
source: Inter-hemispheric inhibition, as assessed by dual-site paired-pulse TMS, is reduced in asymptomatic individuals but with a family history of dystonia (Bäumer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a TMS study.

claim: TDT was found abnormal in Parkinson's disease.
source: A critical issue is that these subclinical physiological alterations may not be specific to dystonia: for example, TDT was found abnormal in Parkinson's disease (Conte et al., 2016) and psychogenic dystonia (Morgante et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited to show the lack of specificity of TDT as an endophenotype.

claim: TDT was found abnormal in psychogenic dystonia.
source: A critical issue is that these subclinical physiological alterations may not be specific to dystonia: for example, TDT was found abnormal in Parkinson's disease (Conte et al., 2016) and psychogenic dystonia (Morgante et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited to show the lack of specificity of TDT as an endophenotype.

claim: Neuroimaging studies demonstrated a pattern of hypermetabolism of the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and supplementary motor area linked with DYT1 and DYT6 dystonia even in nonmanifesting gene carriers.
source: Some neuroimaging studies also demonstrated a pattern of hypermetabolism of the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and supplementary motor area linked with DYT1 and DYT6 dystonia even in nonmanifesting gene carriers (Eidelberg et al., 1998; Trost et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from neuroimaging studies.

claim: Nonmanifesting DYT1 and DYT6 subjects exhibit a combination of rather preserved cerebello-thalamic tract and reduced downstream thalamus-motor cortex tract.
source: While cerebello-thalamic fiber tract integrity in these dystonias is diversely affected in all gene carriers, nonmanifesting subjects exhibit a combination of rather preserved cerebello-thalamic tract and reduced downstream thalamus-motor cortex tract, suggesting that symptom manifestation due to disrupted cerebello-thalamic communication may be prevented by reduced thalamo-cortical interactions, as seen in nonmanifesting carriers (Argyelan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from a neuroimaging study on tract integrity.

claim: Symptom manifestation due to disrupted cerebello-thalamic communication may be prevented by reduced thalamo-cortical interactions in nonmanifesting DYT1 carriers.
source: While cerebello-thalamic fiber tract integrity in these dystonias is diversely affected in all gene carriers, nonmanifesting subjects exhibit a combination of rather preserved cerebello-thalamic tract and reduced downstream thalamus-motor cortex tract, suggesting that symptom manifestation due to disrupted cerebello-thalamic communication may be prevented by reduced thalamo-cortical interactions, as seen in nonmanifesting carriers (Argyelan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the cited neuroimaging study.

claim: The data did not reveal significant increases in neuronal activity in naive Gnal+/- mice that would compare to the hypermetabolism found in DYT1 or DYT6 patients.
source: Although our data did not reveal significant increases in neuronal activity in naive Gnal+/- mice that would compare to the hypermetabolism found in DYT1 or DYT6 patients, we found an anomalously high responsiveness of thalamus VAL neurons to cerebellar stimulations; since we found no difference in DN responsiveness to optogenetic modulations between genotypes, it is likely that this difference results at least in part from an increased synaptic transmission or postsynaptic excitability.
evidence: This is based on the baseline firing rate data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The anomalously high responsiveness of VAL neurons to cerebellar stimulations in Gnal+/- mice likely results at least in part from increased synaptic transmission or postsynaptic excitability.
source: Although our data did not reveal significant increases in neuronal activity in naive Gnal+/- mice that would compare to the hypermetabolism found in DYT1 or DYT6 patients, we found an anomalously high responsiveness of thalamus VAL neurons to cerebellar stimulations; since we found no difference in DN responsiveness to optogenetic modulations between genotypes, it is likely that this difference results at least in part from an increased synaptic transmission or postsynaptic excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased responses without increased DN activity.

claim: Oxotremorine injections affected both control and Gnal+/- mice, but induced dystonic postures only in the mutant mice.
source: Oxotremorine injections affected both control and Gnal+/- mice, but induced dystonic postures in the mutant mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: The oxotremorine-induced reduction of firing in the CL of Gnal+/- mice most likely reflects abnormal activity in the thalamo-striatal pathway in relation with dystonic symptoms.
source: While these injections induced an overall decrease in firing rate in the DN, VAL, and M1 in both genotypes, the reduction in firing rate in the CL was only visible in mutant mice. Since only Gnal+/- mice expressed a strong dystonic phenotype, an oxotremorine-induced reduction of firing may correspond to a rather nonspecific effect of the cholinergic stimulation in the DN, VAL, and M1 while the specific change in the CL of Gnal+/- most likely reflects abnormal activity in the thalamo-striatal pathway in relation with dystonic symptoms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genotype-specific effect in CL.

claim: No difference was observed between genotypes in the reduction of discharge or irregularity of DN neurons under oxotremorine in Gnal+/- mice.
source: We did not observe a difference between genotypes in the reduction of discharge or irregularity of DN neurons under oxotremorine in Gnal+/- mice, nor a decreased excitability to optogenetic stimulations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased irregularity of neuronal discharge is observed in the cerebellar nuclei in murine models of DYT1, DYT12, DYT6 dystonia or from dystonic dt rats.
source: This contrasts with the observations from murine models of DYT1, DYT12, DYT6 dystonia or from dystonic dt rats, where increased irregularity of neuronal discharge is observed in the cerebellar nuclei (LeDoux and Lorden, 1998; Chen et al., 2014; Fremont et al., 2014; Fremont et al., 2017; van der Heijden et al., 2021), as also seen in dystonia caused by cerebellar infusion with kainate (e.g., Pizoli et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from multiple studies on other dystonia models.

claim: Increased discharge irregularity in cerebellar nuclei could be a landmark of dystonia with a primary cerebellar contribution.
source: This increased discharge irregularity could therefore be a landmark of dystonia with a primary cerebellar contribution (LeDoux et al., 1993; Fremont et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the pattern across different models.

claim: Dystonia in Gnal+/- mice might mainly result from the action of oxotremorine in the striatum and hence exhibit fewer abnormalities in the cerebellar nuclei discharge.
source: In contrast to these rodent models, dystonia in Gnal+/- mice might mainly result from the action of oxotremorine in the striatum of Gnal+/- mice (Pelosi et al., 2017) and hence exhibit less fewer abnormalities in the cerebellar nuclei discharge.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known mechanism of dystonia induction in this model.

claim: Studies of integrated measures of connectivity point toward a reduction of the entrainment of the cerebellum over downstream regions in dystonic patients.
source: These studies rather point toward a reduction of the entrainment of the cerebellum over downstream regions (Brighina et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2014; Filip et al., 2017; DeSimone et al., 2019; Porcacchia et al., 2019; Panyakaew et al., 2020; but see Kita et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from multiple studies on cerebellar connectivity in dystonia patients.

claim: A reduction of CBI was found in focal hand dystonia.
source: So far, the significance of these alterations is unclear: while a reduction of CBI was found in focal hand dystonia, it was either reduced or normal in cervical dystonia (Brighina et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2014; Porcacchia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from studies on CBI in dystonia.

claim: CBI was either reduced or normal in cervical dystonia.
source: So far, the significance of these alterations is unclear: while a reduction of CBI was found in focal hand dystonia, it was either reduced or normal in cervical dystonia (Brighina et al., 2009; Koch et al., 2014; Porcacchia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from studies on CBI in dystonia.

claim: In a rodent model of DYT12 dystonia, the cerebello-thalamic tract propagates pathological activities toward the striatum.
source: In a rodent model of DYT12 dystonia, the cerebello-thalamic tract propagates pathological activities toward the striatum (Chen et al., 2014), suggesting that a decreased cerebello-thalamic functionality could exert a protective effect.
evidence: This is cited from a study on DYT12 mice.

claim: A decreased cerebello-thalamic functionality could exert a protective effect in dystonia.
source: In a rodent model of DYT12 dystonia, the cerebello-thalamic tract propagates pathological activities toward the striatum (Chen et al., 2014), suggesting that a decreased cerebello-thalamic functionality could exert a protective effect.
evidence: This is speculation based on the DYT12 findings.

claim: Abnormal involvement of the cerebellum in the motor circuits has been linked to the presence of tremor in dystonia.
source: Abnormal involvement of the cerebellum in the motor circuits has also been linked to the presence of tremor in dystonia (DeSimone et al., 2019), for which accumulating evidence correlates this feature with cerebellar dysfunction (Antelmi et al., 2017; Martino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from studies on tremor in dystonia.

claim: Dynamic causal modeling of brain activity from patients with dystonic tremor suggests a central contribution of the cerebellum and cerebello-thalamic pathway in this form of tremor.
source: Indeed, dynamic causal modeling of brain activity from patients with dystonic tremor suggests a central contribution of the cerebellum and cerebello-thalamic pathway in this form of tremor (Nieuwhof et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from a modeling study.

claim: The functional state of cerebello-thalamic pathway may depend on the type of dystonia.
source: Overall, the functional state of cerebello-thalamic pathway may thus depend on the type of dystonia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variability across different forms of dystonia.

claim: In a type of dystonia with a primary striatal dysfunction, the hyperexcitability of the cerebello-thalamic tract could reveal an increased susceptibility to dystonia.
source: Our results suggest that in a type of dystonia with a primary striatal dysfunction (Pelosi et al., 2017) the hyperexcitability of the cerebello-thalamic tract could reveal an increased susceptibility to dystonia, already present in presymptomatic Gnal+/- mice and further potentiated after the first dystonic episode; a decrease in functional connectivity could however correspond to a long-term adaptation of the cerebello-forebrain pathways, which did not take place in the timescale of our experiments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of the DYT25 model.

claim: A decrease in functional connectivity could correspond to a long-term adaptation of the cerebello-forebrain pathways.
source: Our results suggest that in a type of dystonia with a primary striatal dysfunction (Pelosi et al., 2017) the hyperexcitability of the cerebello-thalamic tract could reveal an increased susceptibility to dystonia, already present in presymptomatic Gnal+/- mice and further potentiated after the first dystonic episode; a decrease in functional connectivity could however correspond to a long-term adaptation of the cerebello-forebrain pathways, which did not take place in the timescale of our experiments.
evidence: This is speculation about potential long-term changes not observed in the study.

claim: In WT mice, θ-burst stimulations of the DN induce a lasting potentiation of responses in downstream structures without affecting the response in the DN.
source: In WT mice, these stimulations induce a lasting potentiation of responses in the downstream structures. They do not affect the response in the DN, indicating that their effect occurs downstream either as an increase in thalamic excitability or as a potentiation of cerebello-thalamic synapses (Aumann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on the findings in Figures 3 and 4 showing potentiation in thalamus/cortex/striatum but not DN.

claim: The effect of θ-burst stimulations in WT mice occurs downstream either as an increase in thalamic excitability or as a potentiation of cerebello-thalamic synapses.
source: In WT mice, these stimulations induce a lasting potentiation of responses in the downstream structures.
